Walkthrough

How to Play Dressmaker

Dressmaker is a cozy crafting game about making one dress, for one person, for one occasion. A customer walks in with a request, you design in your sketchbook, buy fabric, arrange pattern pieces, cut, sew, decorate and hand the dress over.

Reviewed September 21, 2026

  • The loopBrief, design, cut, sew, decorate, hand in
  • Decide firstRead the brief before you design
  • Never skipThe mannequin preview
  • Paid inCoin, reputation and a star rating
  • CuttingPermanent — there is no undo
  • Time to learnAbout 30 minutes to the first good dress

To play Dressmaker, read the customer's brief, design in the sketchbook, choose fabric and color, lay out the pattern, cut, sew, decorate and hand the dress in for coin, reputation and a star rating. Read the brief before you design; preview the layout before you cut.

The five stages

Nothing is timed, and the only things you can lose are cloth and coin.

StageWhat you decideWhat it costs you
SketchbookSilhouette, color, samples, appliquéA design you cannot supply
FabricWhich bolt goes on which panelCloth that fights the design
Layout and cuttingGrain or bias, and piece placementA permanent mark on the dress
SewingSeam order and alignmentPanels that fit together badly
DecoratingButtons, bows, appliqué, laceTrim that buries the fabric

The first five minutes

You start in the shop: counter, fabric shelves, sewing machine, mannequin, sketchbook. No control list is published, so here is the order of play.

  1. 1

    Go to the customer

    read the commission before anything else.

  2. 2

    Open the sketchbook

    every dress starts as a design, not a bolt.

  3. 3

    Check your stock

    samples you cannot buy, you cannot cut.

  4. 4

    Walk the room

    look at the bolts, pet the kitty.

Reading a commission

Every client arrives with an important event to dress for and their own taste — "tailored specially to important events and their individual tastes."

What you needWhere it comes from
The occasionThe customer's own words at the counter
Their tasteThe conversation: colors, reactions, word choice
The numbersThe sketchbook Requirements box

Note

the brief is the only free part of a commission. The full attribute list is unpublished, so target names vary by client.

The sketchbook: designing before you cut

Official wording: you "design and colour your dress in your sketchbook, adding fabric samples and appliqué."

  1. 1

    Silhouette first

    the shape decides your pattern pieces.

  2. 2

    Color second

    free and reversible at this stage.

  3. 3

    Fabric samples third

    so the mock-up uses stock you own.

  4. 4

    Appliqué last

    plan it here, place it after sewing.

Note

the full game carries over 150 dress pieces and over 350 accessories. A silhouette is free to change now and expensive after the cut.

Buying and choosing fabric

The store names cotton, linen, wool, silk and velvet among over 450 fabrics. No stats are published, so judge cloth the way a dressmaker does.

Judge it byWhy it matters
DrapeStiff cloth holds a shape; soft cloth collapses into folds
Print scaleA large print is chopped up the moment you cut a bodice
CostNo price list exists; the bolt you buy is the bolt you must make work
PanelsYou pick the fabric for each panel: a cotton bodice, a silk skirt

Pattern layout: grain, bias and the preview

The official Steam store page puts it plainly: how you arrange and cut out your fabric "is what appears on the final dress."

PlacementAligned to the grainCut on bias
What it isLined up with the threads of the weaveA diagonal cut across that weave
How it behavesStraight, stable, evenMore give and a different hang
When to choose itFor panels that must stay squareAs a deliberate look, never as a fix

Tip

preview every layout on the mannequin before you cut. It is the last free check you get.

Cutting: the point of no return

Plan the whole layout before the first cut.

Warning

cutting is permanent. No seam fixes a panel cut at the wrong angle, and no trim hides a motif sliced in half.

  • Place every piece the design needs, not just the biggest.
  • Check print direction — directional cloth cannot be flipped.
  • Mind the waste — leftover cloth is coin.

Sewing: feeding fabric through the machine

Official wording: "Feed your fabric through the sewing machine to stitch it together." The screenshot caption promises "a sewing machine with infinite bobbin," so there is no spool to manage.

  • Structural seams first — panels must meet edge to edge.
  • No seam sequence is published — think the order through first.

Decorating: buttons, bows, appliqué and lace

Buttons, bows, appliqué and lace trims go on "wherever you like with complete creative freedom."

  • Busy print — keep trim near the edges.
  • Plain silhouette — decoration is where the personality comes from.
  • Three good ideas — a loud print, heavy lace and a big bow compete.

Turning in the dress

Hand the dress to the customer, or sell your own designs off the rack. Story commissions run about 35 hours, excluding off-rack work.

What you doWhat you get
Meet the briefCoin, reputation and a good star rating
Miss the briefLess coin, and you see it in the customer's reaction
Sell off the rackSteady coin, with nobody's wedding depending on it

One official hand-in line reads: "Oh, how wonderful. This is MY dress, exactly as I wanted it."

Note

coin and reputation are the feedback loop. No coin table, reputation threshold or star formula has ever been published.

How your dress is scored

A commission is not judged on vibes: the sketchbook lists named attributes with numeric targets.

Where you see itWhat it looks likeWhat it means
Sketchbook, Requirements boxQuality 70, Flowers 60, Cute 30, Romantic 45What this customer judges you on
Sketchbook, budget800, and roughly 3.85m of fabric requiredWhat you can afford to spend
Fabric shop, commission limitsQuality 0/80, Formal 0/50, Simple 0/75, Professional 0/50Progress against a ceiling
Fabric shop, hard rule"Use only black"Non-negotiable, beats taste
Name card at hand-inA star ratingHow the dress landed, in stars
  • Read the targets before you design. A brief asking for 60 Flowers wants floral cloth and trim.
  • Not every brief names the same attributes. The garden-party commission lists four.
  • Limits are ceilings too. A Simple 0/75 line caps how much decoration the customer wants.
  • Hard rules beat taste. Black only means a pink silk fails.

Note

the two numbers in a limit pair read as progress against a ceiling, but the game never labels them. The attribute list and star formula are unpublished.

Beginner mistakes

MistakeWhy it costs youWhat to do instead
Designing before reading the briefYou build a dress nobody asked forRead the targets, then sketch
Designing a dress you cannot affordCoin spent on cloth that fights the designSettle the fabric in the sketchbook
Rushing the shearsA bad layout shows on the dress foreverPreview, then cut once
Ignoring print scaleA large motif disappears into small panelsBig prints on big panels
Cutting on the bias by accidentBias is a look, not a way to make a piece fitChoose bias on purpose
Over-decoratingTrim buries the fabric you paid forKeep trim near the edges
